title: SEBI Bars Zee's Subhash Chandra and Punit Goenka From Securities Market for One Year
excerpt: India's market regulator imposed ₹1.48 crore in penalties on Zee Entertainment, its CEO, and founder-chairman emeritus after finding company land was secretly pledged for promoter-linked loans.
body:
• SEBI fined Punit Goenka ₹58 lakh, Subhash Chandra ₹60 lakh, and ZEEL ₹30 lakh after finding a Hyderabad property was pledged for promoter-linked loans without board approval.
  • Both Goenka and Chandra are barred from the securities market for one year; ZEEL itself faces a two-month ban.
  • The order lands days before a critical shareholder vote on Zee's second attempt at a ₹3,143 crore promoter-led fundraise via preferential warrants.
  • ZEEL shares fell as much as 10% in early trading on the first session after the order, extending a bruising stretch for the media company's stock.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India on Friday imposed penalties totalling ₹1.48 crore ($155,000) on Zee Entertainment Enterprises, its Chief Executive Punit Goenka, and founder-chairman emeritus Subhash Chandra for securities law violations tied to a Hyderabad land pledge, according to an order published on SEBI's website.

Goenka was fined ₹58 lakh and Chandra ₹60 lakh, while ZEEL was penalised ₹30 lakh, Reuters reported. Both individuals have been barred from the securities market for one year, and the company itself faces a two-month ban.

The Hyderabad Land Case

SEBI's investigation began when title deeds for a ZEEL property in Hyderabad went missing. The regulator found that the land had been used as collateral for loans taken by entities linked to the company's large shareholders — without approval from the board, audit committee, shareholders, or investors.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=EJrJY0hiKU8

"ZEEL's property was deployed for the benefit of related entities and the arrangement was not disclosed to the company's board, audit committee, shareholders or investors," SEBI found in its order, according to Reuters.

The case adds to a long-running pattern of governance investigations at Zee. In 2023, SEBI barred Chandra and Goenka from board positions in listed companies after finding they had diverted funds from ZEEL to related entities. That probe, which uncovered irregularities worth an estimated ₹2,000 crore, traced back to Chandra's letters of comfort used to secure loans from Yes Bank on behalf of related parties.

Fundraise at Risk

The timing of the order is particularly damaging. Zee's board approved a ₹3,143 crore fundraise in early July through the preferential issuance of 24.95 crore fully convertible warrants to Sunbright Mauritius Investments, an entity linked to the Goenka family, at ₹126 per warrant. The plan would raise the promoter group's stake from roughly 4% to over 18%.

This is Zee's second attempt at the same fundraise. Shareholders rejected a near-identical proposal in mid-2025, when only 59.5% voted in favour — well short of the 75% supermajority required for a special resolution.

Proxy advisory firms remain divided ahead of the upcoming vote. SES backed the proposal, arguing that promoters need "skin in the game" and that Zee's competitive position demands fresh capital. InGovern recommended shareholders vote against it, citing "significant promoter-only dilution, embedded optionality in the warrant structure, inadequate justification for the chosen funding route, limited disclosure on promoter financing, and continuing regulatory and accountability overhang," according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

Zee has outlined a detailed capital deployment plan: ₹1,000 crore for sports rights and production, ₹450 crore each for content and technology initiatives and micro-drama, ₹300 crore for kids' edutainment and animation, and ₹944 crore for potential acquisitions.

"The board chose to secure this capital in a single transaction rather than return to shareholders repeatedly over the next three years, and we are confident that is the right approach for the company and for our shareholders."

— Zee Entertainment, in response to proxy firm concerns

Market Reaction and What Lies Ahead

ZEEL shares dropped as much as 10% in the first trading session following the SEBI order, extending a volatile year for the stock. The company has said it is seeking legal advice on the order and has maintained that its fundraising plans remain unaffected.

The ban compounds an already complicated picture for Zee. Public investors hold 96% of the company's shares, with nearly 39% controlled by institutional investors including HDFC Mutual Fund, the Life Insurance Corporation of India, and Norway's Government Pension Fund Global. Any erosion of institutional confidence could be decisive in the warrant vote.

ZEEL, which operates Zee TV, Zee Cinema, and the streaming platform Zee5, secured broadcast rights for the 2026 FIFA World Cup in India earlier this year — a deal intended to anchor its pivot toward sports content. But the recurring governance questions may overshadow commercial progress.

The company can appeal the SEBI order before the Securities Appellate Tribunal, a route Chandra and Goenka have taken in previous rounds of regulatory action. Whether the latest sanctions tip institutional shareholders against the warrant proposal — or whether Zee's growth story proves persuasive enough on the second attempt — will likely be decided in the coming weeks.
